profiles.meeting_scenario: The meeting is a 30-minute coordination check between the surrogate-modeling lead and the simulator integration lead for an internal demo of a warp-optimized Gaussian-process deployment scheduler for nuclear fuel-cycle studies. The project goal is to show that the optimizer can propose reactor deployment schedules for a representative once-through fuel cycle, pass those schedules into a low-fidelity simulator during each optimization loop, and then send selected schedules to a fuller simulation for validation. The agenda is to align on which benchmark case they are using for the demo, what exactly the deployment-schedule handoff artifact contains, when a run should be treated as 'converged' and ready for benchmark submission, and how the simulator output will be returned to the optimizer for the next iteration. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on interfaces, timing, and responsibilities so the next optimization iteration and validation run can proceed without further discussion.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Gaussian process regression, dynamic time warping objectives, sequential design for simulation-guided optimization
members.background: Maya is a staff ML researcher who adapted warped GP regression to propose reactor deployment schedules inside a lightweight fuel-cycle workflow and is responsible for the optimization notebook and demo figures.
members.private_state: She wants the internal demo to match the narrative and numbers from the draft methods note, avoid any extra reformatting work, and preserve the fast outer-loop cadence she has already been showing to the PI.
hidden_assumptions: The 'once-through reference case' is the 200-year paper-reproduction configuration in her experiments repository, because that is the case attached to all of her current plots.

A 'deployment schedule' is just the time-indexed vector of newly deployed reactor counts; initial fleet composition and retirements are inherited from benchmark defaults and do not need to be restated.

A run is only really 'converged' when the outer loop remains under the stated threshold after incorporating full-simulation feedback, ideally for two successive iterations rather than a single low point.
The simulator will return an annual production curve already aligned to the optimizer's yearly grid, because every prior handoff she has used was annualized before she saw it.

members.name: Ethan Alvarez
members.expertise: Fuel-cycle simulation workflows, benchmark packaging, run orchestration, schema validation for deployment inputs
members.background: Ethan is a computational engineer who maintains the lab's low-fidelity simulator wrappers and benchmark submission pipeline, and he is responsible for turning optimizer outputs into simulator-ready inputs and feeding results back into shared storage.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the integration path simple, use the already validated baseline package in his repo, and avoid launching expensive benchmark jobs more times than necessary.
hidden_assumptions: The 'once-through reference case' is the integration baseline YAML in the simulator repo, because that is the only once-through package his adapter currently treats as the standard handoff target.
A 'deployment schedule' should be self-contained enough to replay the run later, so it should travel with initial fleet and retirement-related fields rather than relying on unstated defaults.
For coordination purposes, 'converged' means the optimizer has reached the target threshold once in the low-fidelity loop and is therefore ready to queue the benchmark confirmation run.
Simulator output remains on the simulator's native subannual grid unless someone explicitly requests aggregation, because the old downstream notebook handled the annual resampling automatically.

misalignment_points.topic: Which once-through reference case they mean
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the once-through reference case' as if it is a single shared benchmark package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the paper-reproduction case in her experiments repo: a 200-year once-through reactor deployment setup used for the draft figures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the simulator integration baseline package in his repo: the maintained once-through benchmark configuration he already knows how to run through the wrapper.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each subteam has only one case they habitually call 'the once-through reference case,' so the phrase feels uniquely identifying to both of them and no clarification seems necessary.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the deployment schedule handoff
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss sending 'the deployment schedule' to the simulator as though the artifact boundary is obvious.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a compact time series of incremental reactor builds by year, assuming the benchmark case already supplies initial fleet, retirements, and other static context.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a self-contained schedule package that includes the build counts plus enough initial-fleet and retirement metadata to rerun the case without consulting paper defaults.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are used to the word 'schedule' covering whatever surrounding context their own tooling silently fills in, so the omission of exact fields sounds normal rather than ambiguous.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as converged and ready
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the run will be handed off 'once it converges' or 'when it's under 1%.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means the outer optimization loop has remained below the target after a full-simulation-informed update, effectively demonstrating stable convergence rather than a single transient score.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this means the optimizer has crossed the threshold once in the lightweight loop, which is enough to trigger the benchmark confirmation run.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the same threshold language and both expect the method to converge quickly anyway, so the distinction between a stable stopping condition and a queueing condition stays invisible.

misalignment_points.topic: How the production curve comes back from simulation
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about feeding back 'the production curve' from the simulator to the GP retraining step.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the returned curve will already be annualized and aligned to the optimizer's yearly horizon, ready to drop into the next DTW comparison.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the simulator's native subannual series can simply be placed in the shared output location because downstream analysis has historically handled any aggregation or resampling.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The team has a long habit of saying 'production curve' without naming the time grid, and each person assumes the other is relying on the same inherited preprocessing convention.
